title: Bài sưu tầm 237 - Passage 2: Reading the Swell: The Science of Polynesian Wayfinding
passageHtml:
READING PASSAGE 237

Reading the Swell: The Science of Polynesian Wayfinding

Paragraph 1. Centuries before European mariners routinely ventured out of sight of land, Polynesian sailors were settling islands scattered across a vast triangle of the Pacific Ocean larger than Europe and Asia combined. Double-hulled canoes completed multi-week ocean crossings without magnetic compasses, sextants, or written charts, relying instead on a disciplined system of environmental observation known as wayfinding. Far from drifting at the mercy of currents, early Pacific navigators planned deliberate two-way voyages to distant archipelagos and returned home accurately.

Paragraph 2. At night, the primary guide was a mental star compass learned through years of shoreline training. Rather than memorizing static constellations in the European fashion, wayfinders learned the precise horizon points where roughly two hundred key stars rise and set. Because Earth rotates smoothly, stars climbing above the eastern horizon follow predictable paths across the sky. To keep track of progress without a visible landmark, navigators use a mental framework called etak: the navigator imagines the canoe sitting fixed beneath the heavens while islands glide past along set bearings. By linking a distant reference island to shifting star positions, the sailor simplifies complex speed and drift calculations into a single clear picture.

Paragraph 3. Cloud cover frequently hides the night sky, forcing navigators to shift their attention from the heavens to the sea surface itself. Deep-ocean swells generated by distant trade winds travel across thousands of kilometres in steady, long-wavelength patterns. When these swells strike an underwater slope or island chain, part of their energy bounces back, creating subtle intersecting ripples. Even when fog or darkness obscures the horizon, a trained wayfinder sitting cross-legged on the deck can detect tiny interruptions in the steady pulse and beat of long ocean swells through how the hull rocks. The real skill lies not in spotting huge breaking surf, which is only visible close to shore, but in separating faint, rhythmic island reflections from messy local waves stirred up by afternoon gusts.

Paragraph 4. Preserving so much geographical information without paper demanded specialized memory techniques. Navigation schools embedded star lists, seasonal wind shifts, and island bearings inside rhythmic songs and ancestral stories that locked complex directional sequences into long-term recall. Young trainees spent hours lying on woven mats beside elders, feeling pebble arrangements that represented wave intersections until every sensation became second nature. Such oral archives ensured that an entire community’s maritime knowledge survived across generations.

Paragraph 5. By the mid-twentieth century, colonial schooling and engine-powered boats had pushed traditional wayfinding to the edge of disappearance. Some Western historians even argued that Polynesia had been populated accidentally when fishing crews were blown off course by unpredictable storms and shifting winds. To test whether deliberate navigation really worked, Hawaiian sailors built the traditional voyaging canoe Hōkūleʻa in the 1970s and invited Mau Piailug, one of the last master navigators from Micronesia, to guide them across four thousand kilometres of open sea to Tahiti. Subsequent voyages carrying sealed GPS loggers for verification confirmed that Piailug and his Hawaiian apprentices maintained accurate courses within a few degrees across thousands of kilometres without touching a single modern instrument.

groups.title: Questions 14–18
groups.instructions:

groups.title: Questions 19–23
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the claims of the writer in Reading Passage 237? In boxes 19–23 on your answer sheet, write YES, NO or NOT GIVEN.

groups.title: Questions 24–26
groups.instructions: Choose the correct letter, A, B, C or D. Write the correct letter in boxes 24–26 on your answer sheet.

steps: Đoạn 1: "without magnetic compasses, sextants, or written charts" ↔ mechanical equipment (H).
Đoạn 2: "while islands glide past along set bearings" ↔ distant islands (B).
Đoạn 3: "tiny interruptions in the steady pulse and beat of long ocean swells" ↔ wave rhythm (C).
Đoạn 4: "locked complex directional sequences into long-term recall" ↔ reinforced memory (E).
Đoạn 5: "unpredictable storms and shifting winds" ↔ changing weather (F).

q19.text: European explorers of the eighteenth century relied on more advanced non-instrument skills than Polynesian sailors.

steps: Đoạn 1: Từ nhiều thế kỷ trước khi người châu Âu dám rời xa bờ, người Polynesia đã vượt đại dương mà không cần la bàn hay hải đồ.
Kết luận: Chọn NO.

q20.text: The mental model known as etak treats the vessel itself as the moving point across a fixed grid.

steps: Đoạn 2: Ngược lại: "the navigator imagines the canoe sitting fixed... while islands glide past" (thuyền đứng yên, đảo di chuyển).
Kết luận: Chọn NO.

q21.text: Detecting refracted ocean swells requires paying attention to how the vessel pitches rather than relying on sight.

steps: Đoạn 3: Dù sương mù hay bóng tối che khuất tầm nhìn, người hoa tiêu ngồi trên boong cảm nhận sóng dội qua độ lắc của thân thuyền.
Kết luận: Chọn YES.

q22.text: Older navigators initially refused to teach non-Polynesian researchers the etak system.

steps: Đoạn 5: Bài nhắc việc mời bậc thầy Mau Piailug từ Micronesia sang dạy thủy thủ Hawaii, không hề nói các bậc thầy lớn tuổi từng từ chối dạy cho nhà nghiên cứu ngoài cộng đồng hay không.
Kết luận: Chọn NOT GIVEN.

q23.text: Modern GPS studies have confirmed that experienced wayfinders can keep a steady heading over long distances.

steps: Đoạn 5: Thiết bị GPS niêm phong xác nhận Piailug và học trò giữ hướng chuẩn chỉ lệch vài độ suốt hàng nghìn km.
Kết luận: Chọn YES.

q24.text: Why does the writer mention 'stationary canoe' imagery in the second paragraph?
options: A. to argue that double-hulled canoes travelled too slowly to be measured
B. to show how Polynesian maps copied early European geometric grids
C. to explain a mental frame of reference that simplifies tracking position
D. to emphasize that calm seas were essential for observing rising stars

steps: Đoạn 2: Hình ảnh thuyền đứng yên giúp đơn giản hóa việc tính toán tốc độ và độ trôi phức tạp thành một bức tranh trực quan.
Kết luận: Chọn C.

q25.text: What challenge do wayfinders face when multiple swell patterns overlap?
options: A. Identifying breaking surf at night when shores are still far away
B. Separating gentle island reflections from choppy wind-driven surface waves
C. Measuring water temperature shifts caused by deep ocean currents
D. Remembering which star path corresponds to each seasonal gust

steps: Đoạn 3: Thử thách thực sự là tách được sóng phản xạ mờ nhạt từ đảo khỏi sóng lộn xộn trên mặt biển do gió chiều gây ra.
Kết luận: Chọn B.

q26.text: What point does the writer make about Mau Piailug’s decision in the final paragraph?
options: A. It proved that GPS trackers interfere with traditional maritime memory.
B. It convinced European historians that early Pacific settlement was accidental.
C. It demonstrated that Micronesians used written charts unlike Hawaiians.
D. It helped revive an endangered skill by sharing it across island communities.

steps: Đoạn 5: Nghệ thuật đi biển truyền thống đứng bên bờ vực biến mất, và chuyến đi cùng học trò Hawaii đã chứng minh và hồi sinh tri thức này.
Kết luận: Chọn D.
